readingInstruction: Read Revelation 3:1-22. Jesus speaks to the last three of the seven churches: Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Notice that two churches receive only criticism, one receives only praise, and the best-known verse in the chapter is addressed to a church, not to an individual.
settingTheScene: Sardis was a wealthy city that had twice fallen to surprise attacks because its defenders thought the acropolis was unassailable. Philadelphia, a small and relatively weak city, was known for earthquakes and for being a gateway to the east. Laodicea was a rich banking and textile center, famous for its black wool, an eye salve, and a water supply piped in from hot springs and cold streams that arrived lukewarm. Jesus addresses each church using images drawn from its own setting.
observation: “You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead” (v. 1).
“Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die” (v. 2).
“I have set before you an open door, which no one is able to shut” (v. 8).
“Because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth” (v. 16).
“For you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing” (v. 17).
“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent” (v. 19).
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me” (v. 20).
“The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne” (v. 21).
interpretation:
To Sardis, Jesus holds “the seven spirits of God and the seven stars.” He says, “I know your works. You have the reputation of being alive, but you are dead.” It is the harshest letter, with no commendation. The church looked fine from outside but was spiritually asleep, as the city had been when it fell. “Wake up, and strengthen what remains and is about to die.” They are to remember what they received and heard, keep it, and repent. If not, he will come like a thief. A few in Sardis have not soiled their garments, and “they will walk with me in white, for they are worthy.” The conqueror will be clothed in white, and Jesus “will never blot his name out of the book of life,” but will confess his name before the Father and his angels. This is a promise of security for the faithful.

To Philadelphia, Jesus is “the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut.” There is only praise. “I know that you have but little power, and yet you have kept my word and have not denied my name.” Christ has set before them “an open door, which no one is able to shut,” perhaps for gospel opportunity. He will make those who slander them come and bow down before their feet, and know that he has loved them. “Because you have kept my word about patient endurance, I will keep you from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world.” Interpreters differ on whether this means being kept through trials (as in John 17:15) or removed from them (as taught in some forms of premillennialism); either way, the promise is that Christ guards the faithful. The conqueror will be made “a pillar in the temple of my God,” never to go out of it, and will have written on him the name of God, of the city of God, and Christ’s own new name.

To Laodicea, Jesus is “the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of God’s creation.” There is no commendation here either. “I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were either cold or hot! So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.” Laodicea’s water came lukewarm from afar: not refreshing like cold water or healing like hot. The church’s works were useless. Their self-image was prosperous: “I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing.” But Jesus says they are “wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.” Their remedy is to buy from him gold refined by fire, white garments, and eye salve, answers to the city’s banking, textile, and medical fame. “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline, so be zealous and repent.”

Then the most famous verse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.” This is often used as an invitation to unbelievers, but its original setting is Christ knocking on the door of his own church. He is on the outside of a congregation that thinks it needs nothing. The invitation to repent and renew fellowship, symbolized by a shared meal, applies to every church and every believer who has drifted. The final promise is the highest of all: “The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne.” The letters end as they began, with the call to hear. Christ does not just judge his churches; he loves them and calls them back.
connection: Matthew 24:42-44 and 1 Thessalonians 5:2-6 speak of coming like a thief. Isaiah 22:22 is the source of the key of David. Isaiah 45:14 and 49:23 are behind the bowing at their feet. Isaiah 60:14 speaks of enemies bowing. John 17:15 prays that the Father would keep believers from the evil one. Colossians 4:13-16 mentions Laodicea. Hosea 12:8 and 1 Corinthians 4:8 speak of self-satisfaction. Proverbs 3:11-12 and Hebrews 12:5-11 speak of the Lord’s discipline. Song of Solomon 5:2 has a similar knocking at the door. Luke 12:35-37 and John 14:23 speak of fellowship with Christ. Luke 22:28-30 promises a share in his throne.
application:
Honestly ask: if people could see your inner spiritual life, would they say you are alive? Pick one thing to strengthen that is about to die.

Open the door to Christ for an area of your life where you have been self-sufficient. Tell him you need him.

Thank Christ for the discipline you may be experiencing as a sign of his love.
prayerPrompts: Ask Jesus to wake you up where you are asleep.
Thank him for the open door he has set before you.
Ask him for the courage to open your door to him.
